utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear the massacre of Serb civilians, mostly women, children, and old men, towards the end of May in the neighbourhood of Krusevica in the area of Raska Gora which was carried out by the members of the HOS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know mean these armed forces of the HOS primarily used multiple rocket launchers to set on fire the Serb Orthodox cathedral and when they destroyed the church in Bilusine [phoen] as well as the old Serb school and old Serb church erected in 1833?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this is an area I know well, the old Serb church was blown up by dynamite, so there weren't any multiple rocket launchers involved. The old Serb church was blown up, also when the JNA was withdrawing from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this down by HOS or by the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that in November 1993 the Croatian forces used tank grenades to destroy the old stone bridge that was the symbol of the town of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a lot of the media were accusing the Army of Republika Srpska of having done that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who did that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, everybody knows. The entire world knows who Praljak is and what he did. So there's no need to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the HOS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what formation is concerned, I really don't know. But it is certain that Praljak issued the order. Now, whether they are the HVO or the HOS, I really don't know. As a matter of fact, I don't think it was the HOS, because after Blaz Kraljevic was killed in Western Herzegovina, on the right bank where the Croats were it was the HVO that was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, the Croat Defence Council, they did that; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know when the JNA units from all of Bosnia-Herzegovina withdrew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say they withdrew from the area of Mostar in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I gave the exact date, the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is to the best of your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I saw. No. I don't know when they got the order, but the artillery and other heavy weaponry was taken out of the airport in Heliodrom and that's what I saw on the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have very little time left. Now, do you know that the Muslims in mid-June 1992 in Podvelezje massacred Colonel Tomo Pusara who during the preceding months provided protection to them and gave them food supplies and other things they needed? This was a well-known incident.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Together with him, his driver Sasa Indjic was killed. Yes, I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that he was -- supplied them with food and protection, supplied them generally in the months that went before that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know, but I wasn't actually there in the field during those months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 30, you take about a camp, a training camp, in fact, at Boracko Lake. And as far as I was able to understand, they had collected up recruits from Konjic and the villages around Boracko Lake. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that it was at the lake that you saw Franko Simatovic, who came to visit there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, is it true that you never had any document to officially confirm that you were a member of those formations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I never did have a document. Neither did any of the others who were there. I'm talking about the guys from Borac and Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm talking about too. That's what I'm saying. Those Red Berets that you describe have nothing to do with the Red Berets of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true, because I saw with my very own eyes the official ID cards of state security issued to the name of Pero Divljak, both the red variety and the blue variety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about your blue and red variety, but this Pero Divljak of yours couldn't have had an official ID card.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know from Tito's Yugoslavia, a state security ID card is not a lottery ticket and can't be bought at a kiosk anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course that's quite true. But he couldn't have had an ID, because as you say, he was a criminal.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were all criminals. There was no difference among them. And as I say, all of them had ID cards. But I happened to see Pero Divljak's.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you saw Pero Divljak's, but you say that he was taken out of the court. I assume that nobody can be taken out of prison without a court order.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be normal in a normal state and country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that in Serbia we didn't have a proper state?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying, in comparison to the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that you were not registered in a single unit in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right; quite true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said you were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to my review of the list, your name wasn't on any one of them. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So how could you have been exchanged without being on any exchange list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in my statement, and when I read through my statement there was some things that weren't correct. But let me explain. The people who helped me were Croats, in fact, from Mostar. And they had --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This section was in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff asked you whether you knew anything about some checkpoints or, rather -- yes, checkpoints, towards Montenegro and in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your answer was - and I made a note of it - "There were countless checkpoints of that sort because anybody and everybody had their checkpoints set up close to their homes, houses."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, if people were guarding their houses and protecting their houses, was it every little nobody who did this living along the border with Bosnia-Herzegovina? Were these all nobodies, as you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question was: Who were they protecting their homes from? Because it was 50 kilometres in depth of the territory. Now, the reason I called them nobodies - and they are, in fact, nobodies - is that they were people who had left Mostar and had been forced to stay up at the lines, the frontlines, to protect these lines of some sort; whereas, the local ones that made a show of manning the checkpoints to control who knows whom just did that to be able to remain, because they weren't allowed to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you said that everybody had a checkpoint in front of their own houses.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, don't take me literally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you describe at one point when asked directly -- I think you said something to the effect that what was going on had something to do with Belgrade, something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what connection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you were asked quite specifically how come you knew that the deserters were being arrested in Montenegro, that this had something to do with Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And your explanation was as follows - and I made a note of that - this is what you said: "In Montenegro, they arrested or the Yugoslav police arrested people in Montenegro. They did the arresting. Whereas, the police of Republika Srpska came up to the border and took the deserters off to prison."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, my first question is this: In Montenegro, they had the Montenegrin police; right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't see it that way, because the period we're talking about, which is 1994, I think Serbia and Montenegro were still called Yugoslavia. Or am I wrong on that score?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yugoslavia, yes. But where do you get this idea from according to which somebody arrests deserters on Montenegrin territory on the basis of an order from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, well, as far as that's concerned, I explained why. The country's name was Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But the Ministry of the Interior, the Ministries of the interior, there was the Ministry of Serbia and the Ministry of the Interior of Montenegro. I assume you know that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are not familiar institutions. As far as I'm concerned. I never had anything to do with the law, so I don't actually know about that. But as you're asking me about these arrests in Montenegro, I can confirm that there were people in prison in Lukavica with me who were brought in from Subotica, Novi Sad, Belgrade, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm talking about. I'm not talking about whether deserters were arrested. I'm saying that you're drawing the conclusion that these orders came from Belgrade, that Belgrade ordered deserters to be arrested on the basis of the fact that you were actually arrested in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Never mind. Let's move on. Is it true that you heard that in this unit, the unit that you mention, under the name of the White Wolves, that mercenaries fought within that unit? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at page 33 of your statement now, please, if you will, the last paragraph, which reads as follows: "At that time during the -- Srdjan Knezevic was in charge of the White Wolves. The White Wolves were made up of mercenaries of many nationalities. For example, in my room, seven different languages were spoken. I remember that in my unit we had people from Russian --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 182, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Naval sabotage unit, for example. Then there were Romanians that had formerly been members of the Securitat, members of a Bulgarian parachute unit, criminals from Cyprus, and local Serbs." So that's what you say. That's the whole paragraph. And I quoted you. It begins, "At that time the White Wolves." And I asked you whether they were mercenaries and you said no. Whereas here you said they were, they comprised of mercenaries.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you saw the corrections that were made to the statement. Now, as far as these misunderstandings with respect to translations goes, I have nothing to do with that. I know exactly what I said. Now, as far as the criminals were concerned, that is quite true. As for the naval diversionary units from Russia, I said that with respect to Jure Rus, who was one of them, Jure the Russian. So I know exactly what I said. They were not mercenaries. They were people fleeing from something. And Dima was the ex-Securitat member, the Romanian, Dima. That was his story. And what I recounted here was on the basis of what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So do you want to say that this has not been correctly interpreted and you put that correction into the statement, they were not mercenaries? Is that what you claim?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has said that in his corrections, which have been attached to the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We've cleared that up now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I must say that this is the first time I hear about all these different nationalities, the Russians, Romanians, Bulgarians et cetera.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never in my life did I encounter anything like that until I arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, then. So there was one Russian man.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several Russians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Several Russians. How many Bulgarians, how many Romanians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two Bulgarians, one Romanian, and several of them from Cyprus. I can't remember exactly. It was a unit which, as I have already stated, was made up of people from outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they volunteers from different countries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that they were volunteers as far as the unit was concerned, but I can only say that as far as Srdjan Knezevic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, is it true that this unit of the White Wolves didn't take part in committing any crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, up to my last day, that is true and correct, because the unit was generally stationed in the Treskavica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it did not take part in committing any crimes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right; it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that they were part of the corps, the special units of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement on page 35 you say that "In the winter of 1994, the White Wolves captured some Muslims who were smuggling cigarettes," et cetera, "and that on that occasion you saw that four men were dead, the fifth was still alive, and he was killed later on allegedly, and that all that had been committed by a man named Petar, one Petar." Did you see him do -- commit all those things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put you right first. It says: "In the winter of 1994 was the only time while I was in the White Wolves unit." So the White Wolves never captured anybody. And I'm talking about the time I was there, while I was with the White Wolves in the winter of 1994. What happened was with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they didn't do this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see it happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That the police committed this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember what the place was called exactly. It was a feature of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about this feature, but which local police force was in charge in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Trnovo police, in collaboration with the police station of Kula in Sarajevo, because they had a mixed battalion together with the army. I really can't tell you more than that. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So these were men from Trnovo and Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And I've already said that it was the Sarajevo Romanija Corps which was in charge, as far as I know, of Trnovo, and that they set up this mixed battalion where there were members of the police force and the commander was Cedo Sladoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll skip over a few questions that could disclose your identity. Just tell me this: At the beginning of 1995, you took part in two military operations, one in Mala Orliste and the other one at Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as far as I was able to gather, there was a strong clash and your unit, as you yourself say, lost 12 men in the space of ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they suffered serious casualties and losses. Is it true that the battles at Debelo Brdo was held without the authorisation of General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this, please: You mentioned a certain man by the name of Ribic, nicknamed Kanada, who when the NATO bombing started captured one or two UNPROFOR soldiers and tied them to the bridge in Pale, seized the UN vehicle, et cetera. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And taking of hostages at that time was rampant; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you link this up, as you explained to us today here, to the fact that you saw Stanisic later on and members of the police unit from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I heard about that from Captain Cvoro. And it was shown on television, it was broadcast. But the first information I received was from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, let's clear this matter up. Do you know, are you aware, that Stanisic was sent from -- by me and it was broadcast that he was going as my special envoy to take these people over because we were holding negotiations with the leadership of Republika Srpska, that they had to set the hostages free?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as that is concerned, I can only repeat what I've already said. The first information I received from Captain Cvoro, the rest was broadcast over television, but I didn't attach any importance to it. I do know that Jovica Stanisic was sent from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to take over the hostages, or rather, to have them released ultimately.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my statement, I describe and state what I know about those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what it says in your statement is not very clear. That's why I wanted to get clarifications from you, because this was a well-known occurrence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you want me to explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said that they were linked to this taking of hostages in some way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All I said was that when the hostages were taken and when all this -- this incident began, that the first information that reached me, because Srdjan on that same day in the evening went to be informed at Lukavica of this event. At that time, I myself went to the military police building. And the first information that reached me as to the takeover of the hostages by Jovica Stanisic or whoever was the envoy sent to do that, I heard this from Captain Cvoro. That's all that I say in my statement; nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did you hear that they had been sent to take over the hostages and release them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the release of hostages, no. But that they had been sent to take over the hostage, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were not there with any unit. All he had was his own security detail. Because the agreement on the release of hostages had been reached by political means. There was no combat operation there. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear of any combat operations in that connection, nor did I see any of them to be able to claim anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said on page 38 that members of the DB of Serbia confiscated the equipment that your unit had taken from the UNPROFOR soldiers. That is, you had to return the equipment that you had taken from UNPROFOR. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as that is concerned, that is the specific unit of which I was a member. I know that Srdjan received an order to return the jeeps, because it was the jeeps that were most frequently taken. As far as the state security of Serbia is concerned, I must repeat: All I know is what I heard from Cvoro, because they confiscated equipment from everyone. This was a whole wave of hostage-taking from Pale to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the had to return all that back.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll leave out a number of questions relating to you personally, because we don't have time to go into private session again. On page 40, you say that a friend of yours who was working in the security of a certain person, who was not a state official - I won't mention the name so as not to reveal your identity - told you that I, after coming to power, wanted to form a unified Serbian police. Did they entrust this task to this friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said here what he told me. I didn't say that you had entrusted him with that task. It says here quite loud and clear that he told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On pages 41 and 42, you mention the camp at Knin, the Knin fortress, Fruska Gora, Golubic, Bruska, Jodankovic [phoen], Kula, in Vojvodina, Lokor -- no, Tara, Mitrovac. Did you personally see all those training centres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really think it's clear. I can't keep on explaining one and the same thing 50 times. I stated quite loud and clear how I know about those camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you know nothing about the Knin fortress or who was in command in Knin or who was in command of the Red Berets in Knin as early as 1990, where they were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know, I said how I learnt about it and from whom. So most of those stories come from Pero Divljak and members of the Red Berets who were there at the Boracko Jezero or lake. So I heard all these things from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see, so you heard everything from them. But let's hurry up to clear up a few more points. You spoke about various civilian lorries coming to the warehouses at Pale, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that this was very frequent.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how much aid in food, clothing, medicines, and every other necessity for the life of people was sent from Serbia? Where did your assumption come from that those lorries were bringing weapons and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But, for instance, if I see a bullet with the inscription "PPU" 1994, standing for Prvi Partizan Uzice, as far as I know Uzice is in Serbia, or maybe I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There's no need for any sarcasm. The PPU is a factory manufacturing ammunition. It was well known in the world, not only in Yugoslavia. So that is not at issue at all. You could have found those bullets in any warehouses.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the year is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that you saw that year. I think you made it up.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the contrary, I know that they had problems in the Army of Republika Srpska because the munition that they had there and most of -- largest warehouses of equipment and ammunition from the former SFRY were in Bosnia -- they had problems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're just wasting time, you telling the witness what you claim to know about. He's told you what his evidence is. Now, you've got two minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I only have two minutes left -- I just need to leaf quickly through my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Kasindol, you saw Mauzer and representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Mauzer in Kasindol, and representatives of the Republic of Srpska Krajina I saw at the Kosuta Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see, both. This one was from Bijeljina and the other from the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And there was a unit called Scorpions. Where did you get the idea that this was a unit of the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is information I received from people I spoke to. And it says in my statement who I talked to up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me just clear up one point, which I think has some broader significance. You spoke about Perisic's speech when the JNA was withdrawing from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you said that the people who were from the area and who wanted to stay behind could stay behind and that they could keep their weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was -- were they, the people who were later transformed into the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the JNA withdrew or, rather, pulled out. The soldiers who were from the territory of Serbia and Montenegro left. Whereas, the people from the area stayed behind with their equipment and that was the way in which the Army of the Republika Srpska was formed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is very important to establish that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that the Red Berets participated in certain battles around Zeleni Jadar and Srebrenica. When was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I saw on the map, the map of Zeleni Jadar, Rudnik, Osmaca, Zepa, and Srebrenica, the whole area, was in Srdjan Knezevic's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there. That was in 1995 -- no, I'm sorry, 1994 in the winter. And this operation, I think, took place in 1993, around Christmastime, because at that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to clear up that your mention of Srebrenica has nothing to do with the events in Srebrenica in 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it hasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we have word that this witness must leave today, so we'll have to limit the time. If you can deal with it in five minutes and we'll give the Prosecution five minutes to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, give me, please, at least a couple of minutes more, because there are so many topics. I have chosen only two which I think are important. I should first like to ask the Witness C-017, with all due respect for his right to express himself in accordance with his feelings, which is -- which every individual is entitled to, when he was asked what ethnicity he was, he said he was a Yugoslav. At a time when there is even no third Yugoslavia left. But that is not why I'm asking him this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 17th of May, 2000, that is three years ago, when he was asked as to what ethnicity he was, he said he was a Serb. And today he says he's a Yugoslav, when even the last Yugoslavia no longer exists. How can he explain that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't matter. Does it really matter now, how he describes himself? But since you've been asked, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem. Even then I declared myself to be a Yugoslav. However, when my statement was taken, they asked me specifically what nationality I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. In the examination-in-chief, you said that in May 1991 you were in a barracks in Zagreb and that fire was opened on JNA soldiers that were killed in front of the barracks and that the barracks was surrounded; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you also said that you didn't know whether other barracks in Croatia were also surrounded.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in your statement here- this is paragraph 49 of the English version- you spoke about the liberation of the JNA barracks in Capljina. Was that barracks in Capljina surrounded for it to have to be deblocked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barracks in Capljina, which was the operation of the parachute brigade in 1993, that is not in Croatia. It's in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is slightly south of Mostar, near Neum. Was that barracks surrounded and then the barracks had to be liberated, as well as the men inside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly happened inside, but I do know that the parachute unit performed an assault attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about what happened to you in Slovenia and you said you couldn't defend yourself because you had rubber bullets.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that many soldiers were killed in Slovenia because they didn't have combat ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear about it. I watched it. They were given -- they weren't given the proper ammunition to be able to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally spent more than two hours lying under a tank or an armoured vehicle - I can't remember which - for more than two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in order to calm things down you spoke to former JNA officers who had abandoned the JNA and joined Slovenian Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that quite a number of officers switched sides while I was still there. But who spoke to whom, I don't know. Who negotiated with whom, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did the same apply to the people living in Bosnia with the JNA. When they switched to the Bosnian army in Krajina though they had personally been members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have something to ask you in connection with paragraph 175. You were saying that the Muslims managed to get some artillery weapons and other equipment partially from what the JNA had left behind and partially from what they were given by the Croats. So do you know that out of the weapons that the JNA could not take with it the Muslim army kept for itself a part of the weaponry of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what about this reference to what was given to them by the Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what exactly they were given by the Croats, but I know that in those days they were acting together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really don't have enough time, though I would have many questions of interest to you and my time is limited, so I'm forced to refer to something in paragraph 156, which has already been discussed. But I need to come back to it. I would like to ask Your Honours to bear in mind points 4 to 7 of the indictment, paragraphs 36, extermination, killings, and murder, and the Prosecution has not given any information linked to this event that the witness witnessed. I think this needs to be assessed, especially in the light of what he said. And he said the following: "I saw Pero Divljak killing with a knife at least ten civilians. I saw numerous men being stabbed several times, then thrown on the ground and shot several times with a pistol."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that what you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it's written down there, but all the acts that you have enumerated I saw myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like the Prosecution to provide evidence of some such thing happening, any of these things actually happening, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has given evidence about it, and we'll have to assess it in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Five minute, please, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have only one question to the witness, and it actually refers to that massacre that he has described and of which Mr. Milosevic mentioned to you during cross-examination it didn't take place, and only -- because we didn't have much time to check, I can only provide something to the witness. It's an official report that we have in our rules of the road files. It's about Mostar and the mass graves in Mostar. And unfortunately, we don't have any -- any Serbian version because we didn't think it would come up in this way. But the witness can read English.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And actually, the only thing I wanted to refer you to, witness, is the reference on page 3, the mass grave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's have copies of it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. It's a document called "Mass grave in Mostar," and it's obviously a report that we have in our rules of the road files. And it's a chronology of events with some mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I only would like you to look at the mass graves Uborak [phoen], mentioned on page 3. And it says here, "On August 27, 1992, the examination -- exhumation of 88 killed civilians at the city garbage dump Uborak in the northern part of the town began. All the deceased were civilians from the city quarters of Vrapcici, Kutiljevac, and Zalik." And there is a list of 54 names of, as I can see, mostly Muslim people. And if you look through this -- briefly through this list of 54 of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, can we know, first of all, where Uborak is?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know -- yes. Witness, can you answer this? Uborak, where is it? It says in the northern part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And if we look at tab 4, that's actually the location --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we have the witness briefly shown tab 4. That's the sketch of the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have here, as you had indicated, a little circle. And it says here Bakina Luka. Is that what is now referred to as Uborak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the area stretching from Bakina Luka upwards. It is this area here. I don't know how to explain it to you, but it is this region over here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's the wider region, as you just showed, the wider region, upwards this word "Bakina Luka" at the river banks. And it refers here to three different quarters, city quarters. Those three quarters, where would they be? We have here only Zalik indicated on this map, tab 4. But the other two, where would that be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Which other districts are you referring to? When I was testifying about the massacre, I spoke only about Zalik.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. But in this document where you find this sentence with the mass grave Uborak, there's a reference to Zalik but also to other places, that is Vrapcici and Kutiljevac. Where would that be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, my mistake. I was looking at the map. Vrapcici and Kutiljevac are on the road from Mostar towards Sarajevo. These are the first two districts on the outskirts of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And is that close to Zalik? Would we see that on --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-017 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think that we should stop now. And no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Dealing with these documents. First of all --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honour, I forgot. I would like to tender this documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm just going to deal with it. I'm not sure we're in the position to accept this as a document. We might mark it for identification, since we've got absolutely no evidence as to what it is. Let's just let me consider.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just -- just to inform you, I was just told that this document comes from the Mostar cantonal court. It was sent to the Prosecution office as the rules of the road file and the -- there is Ivica Kostovic who signs this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can just raise a matter. Evidentially at this stage, in my submission, the witness can -- can mention a name and confirm something in the document, but I don't think that it causes then the document to become an exhibit, because it has no real reference point from this witness in his testimony. We simply don't know where it came from, where it arose, what it's to do with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we've just heard it's from the court. It would seem to me that if some evidence can be produced that it is from the court, it's admissible. At the moment, we've merely got something to the effect that it's from the head of the department of information and research. If that can be confirmed in some way, that it comes from the court, we'll admit it. I suggest what we do at the moment is we mark it for identification, we give it the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution Exhibit 461, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document speaks about people who were buried. It cannot automatically be linked to an event that the witness saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we recognise -- let me interrupt you. We recognise that. All it can do is to prove, if it's admitted, which at the moment it isn't - it's merely marked for identification - all it can prove is that there was an exhumation. Now, whether we choose to link it with the event or not will depend on other evidence. It's no -- worth no more than what it actually says. That's the case with any form of evidence. We've also got here - let me deal with this next - the statement. I must say, speaking for myself, I don't think we really need it exhibited. And in those -- unless -- Mr. Kay, do you want to say anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, I don't think it should be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we don't think it's taken things far enough. What we'll do is return the statement and withdraw it from the bundle. Let me make one final point before we let the witness go. To those watching and those reporting the proceedings today, that references to where this witness is from have been redacted and should therefore not be reported. Witness C-017, that does conclude your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
